title: Chapter 1: Your First Program and Your AI Study Partner
video_title: Python Chapter 1: Your First Program and Your AI Study Partner
summary: Follow Asha as she builds a receipt for her family's Corner Cafe: install Python, write and run a first program, control output with print, sep and end, and read error messages. Then watch her add an order code with an AI assistant at all six stages (plan, write, generate, test, debug and improve), catching two AI mistakes by checking.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly.
The cafe's till, a train timetable and a calculator all run programs.
AI can write code. It is often right, and sometimes wrong while sounding sure.
**You** run the code. **You** decide if it is correct.

segments.say: A program is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly.
The till at Asha's cafe runs one. So do train timetables and calculators.
AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Claude can write code. They are often right. Sometimes they are wrong, and still sound sure.
So you are the one who runs the code, and decides if it is correct.

scenes.title: The idea: Python reads from top to bottom
scenes.direction: Teach the model with the diagram, the two key words and the recipe, then check it with a quiz, then a breather.

visual.heading: How Python runs a program
visual.label: The idea
body: The **interpreter** reads your `.py` file and carries out each line in order.
visual.pre:
You write          Python reads          The computer acts
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
 | hello.py  | ---> |  line 1      | ---> | shows line 1      |
 | (text)    |      |  line 2      |      | shows line 2      |
 +-----------+      +--------------+      +-------------------+
                     top to bottom,
                     one line at a time

segments.say: Here is the big idea. A Python program is a text file that ends in dot p y.
Python, the program called the interpreter, reads it and carries out each line in order: top to bottom, one line at a time.

visual.heading: Two words you need
visual.label: Key words
items: A **function** is a named action Python already knows. Call it with its name and brackets: `print(...)`.
A **string** is text inside quotation marks: `"Hello"`.

segments.say: Print is a function: a named action that Python already knows. You call it with its name, then brackets.
And text inside quotation marks is called a string.

visual.heading: A program is like a cafe recipe
visual.label: Analogy
items: The cook follows each step in order, exactly as written.
Where it stops working: a cook can guess what you meant. Python cannot.
A typing mistake makes Python stop and report an error.

segments.say: Think of a recipe card in Asha's kitchen. The cook follows each step in order.
The comparison stops at one point. A cook can guess what you meant. Python cannot.
One typing mistake, and Python stops with an error.

visual.question: A file has three `print()` lines. In which order does Python run them?
options: All three at the same time
From top to bottom, one line at a time
visual.explain: Python runs one line at a time, from the first line to the last.

segments.say: Let's check that idea. A file has three print lines. In which order does Python run them?

after.say: B. From top to bottom, one line at a time.

items: A program is a list of instructions.
Python runs it from top to bottom.
Text in quotation marks is a string.

visual.heading: Step 1: Install Python
visual.label: Build it

segments.say: Step 1: install Python. Get the latest version. Any version from 3.12 works for this course.
On Windows, use the Python install manager from python dot org or the Microsoft Store.
On macOS, download the installer package from python dot org.
On Linux, Python is usually installed already.
Then open a terminal and check the version.
On Windows, type python, space, dash dash version.
On macOS and Linux, type python3 instead. You should see a line that starts with Python 3.

scenes.title: Steps 2 and 3: Asha's first program
scenes.direction: The file types itself in, line by line. Then the run command, then the output.

visual.heading: Step 2: Asha's first program
visual.hidden_text: Run it to see the output.

segments.say: Step 2. Asha opens a code editor, such as Visual Studio Code or IDLE, and creates a file called ex 0 1 hello.
Line 1 starts with a hash sign, so it is a comment. Python ignores it. Comments are notes for people.
Line 2 prints a greeting with her name.
Line 3 prints a second line.
Step 3: run it. In the terminal, go to the folder that holds the file.
On Windows, type python, then the file name.
On macOS and Linux, type python3, then the file name.
And there it is: two lines. Each print makes one line of output.
The quotation marks do not appear. They only mark where the text starts and ends.

scenes.title: Step 4: Order matters
scenes.direction: Use the cafe's tea recipe. The steps type in, then the learner predicts the order, then the reveal.

segments.say: Step 4. Asha writes the cafe's tea recipe as a program. Step 1, boil the water.
Step 2, add the tea leaves.
Step 3, pour the tea into a cup.
You know how Python reads a file. Use that now.

ask.question: In which order will the three steps appear in the output?

after.say: The same order as the code. Step 1, step 2, step 3.
Swap two lines in your file and run it again. The output changes, because Python always runs from top to bottom.

scenes.title: Step 5: Spacing with sep and end
scenes.direction: Teach the two settings first, then the code, then the prediction, then a quick check, then a breather.

visual.heading: Step 5: Two settings of `print()`
visual.label: Build it
rows: What goes after the last value

segments.say: Step 5. The receipt needs neat spacing, so Asha learns two settings. Print can show several values, separated by commas.
Sep sets what goes between the values. By default, it is one space.
End sets what goes after the last value. By default, it is a new line.
Line 2 has a calculation, 3 plus 4, with no quotation marks.
Line 3 prints the cafe's opening time, and sets sep to a colon.
Line 4 sets end to three dots, and line 5 prints the word done.

ask.question: What do lines 4 and 5 print together?

after.say: Line 2 prints 7, because Python calculates anything without quotation marks.
Line 3 joins the values with colons, so they look like a time.
And line 4 ends with three dots instead of a new line, so line 5 continues on the same line: Loading, dot dot dot, done.

visual.question: Which setting changes what goes **between** the values in `print()`?
visual.explain: `sep` is the separator between values. `end` is what comes after the last value.

segments.say: Quick check. Which setting changes what goes between the values?

after.say: B, sep. Sep goes between. End goes after.

items: You can run a Python file.
Each `print()` makes one line.
`sep` goes between values; `end` goes after them.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one receipt

visual.heading: Three safety habits
visual.label: Before you start
items: Never paste passwords, keys or private information into an AI tool.
Run every piece of AI code yourself, and compare it with what you asked for.
You are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

segments.say: Before Asha opens an AI assistant, she follows three safety habits.
One. Never paste passwords, keys or private information.
Two. Run every piece of AI code yourself, and compare it with what you asked for.
Three. You are responsible for the code you use, even if an AI wrote it.

messages.text: I am a beginner. My Python receipt prints a cafe name, items and a total. I want to add an order code, CAFE-1024-T4, under the cafe name. List the steps in plain English. No code yet.

1. Find the line that prints the cafe name.
2. Add one new print line after it.
3. Print the three parts of the code as three values, with hyphens between them.
4. Run the receipt and check the code, character by character.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Before any code, Asha asks how to add the order code. She says what she wants, and says: no code yet.
The AI answers with four clear steps. Each one is something she can check. A plan you understand is easier to check than code you do not.

visual.heading: Write it, then ask for an explanation

messages.text: Before I change my receipt, explain it to me. Do not rewrite it. One simple sentence for each group of lines.

Lines 2 to 4 print the header between two borders, so the order code goes after line 3.
Lines 5 and 6 use `sep` to put dots between each item and its price.
Lines 7 and 8 calculate `1 + 1` and `3 + 7`, so Python prints 2 and 10.
Lines 9 and 10 close the receipt.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Before she changes her receipt, Asha makes sure she understands every line. She asks the AI to explain her code, not to rewrite it.
The AI explains each group, and shows where the order code belongs: after line 3. Asha checks each sentence against what she learned.

visual.heading: Generate code with a precise request

messages.text: Write one line of Python that prints the order code `CAFE-1024-T4`, using three separate values. Show the output too.
Here is the code. It prints `CAFE-1024-T4`.
I ran the AI's line. This is what it printed:

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Now Asha asks for the code line itself: one line that prints the order code with hyphens.
The AI gives a line of code, and says it prints the order code with hyphens. It sounds sure.
Look at its code. You learned exactly what this line does in step 5.

ask.question: The AI says this prints `CAFE-1024-T4`. Is it right? Why?

after.say: Asha runs it. It prints spaces, not hyphens. The AI was wrong, and it sounded sure. Can she find out why? That is what testing is for.

visual.heading: Test: compare expected and real output

messages.text: I expected `CAFE-1024-T4`. The line printed `CAFE 1024 T4`. List every difference, character by character.

There are two differences. Characters 5 and 10 are spaces, but you expected hyphens.
The cause: `sep` is a space by default. Add `sep="-"`.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha gives the AI what she expected, and what the line really printed.
This time the AI finds both differences, and names the cause: sep is a space by default. It adds sep equals hyphen.
Asha does not trust it yet. She runs it. Now the order code is correct, so she adds it to her receipt.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: I added the order code to my receipt and got this error. Here are the last two lines of my code. First explain the cause and the line. Then show the smallest fix.

The cause is on line 11: `Print` starts with a capital P. Python names are case-sensitive, so `Print` is not the `print()` function.
The fix: change `Print` to `print`.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. While adding the order code, Asha types Print with a capital P on the last line. Python stops with an error. She pastes her code and the full error.
She asks for the cause first, then the smallest fix. The AI names line 11, explains that names are case-sensitive, and changes one letter.

messages.text: Review my receipt for readability. Here are the order code and price lines. Suggest at most two improvements, each with a one-sentence reason. Do not change what it prints.

1. Add a comment that says what the program does, such as a cafe receipt with its order code. A reader then knows its purpose at once.
2. The dots do not line up. Make both `sep` values the same length.
I counted: both price rows are already 23 characters, so they do line up. Suggestion 2 is wrong. I added the comment and ran the receipt:

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. The receipt now works. Asha asks for at most two readability suggestions, each with a reason.
Suggestion 1 helps. Suggestion 2 says the dots do not line up.
Asha checks it herself. She counts: both price rows are 23 characters, so they already line up. The AI was wrong again. She keeps suggestion 1 only, and runs the receipt.

segments.say: Here is the result. A comment that says what the program does, on line 2. And the order code, on line 5.
Every stage helped, and at every stage Asha checked the answer herself. That is how you work with AI.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Teach three mistakes with their real error reports, then let the learner spot the fourth, then a summary table and a quick check.

segments.say: Mistake 1. The closing quotation mark is missing, so Python cannot see where the text ends.
It reports a syntax error. That means Python could not read the file, so no line runs at all.
The fix: add the closing quotation mark. Remember this rule: every opening mark needs its closing partner, for quotation marks and for brackets.
Mistake 2 is the one Asha debugged with the AI. Print with a capital P is a different name. Here it is in a short test file.
Notice that Start printed first. This error happened while the program was running, so the lines above it had already run.
The report names line 3, and the last line even suggests the fix.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: curly quotation marks
visual.note: Curly: `“ ”`   Straight: `" "`   Python accepts only the straight ones.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Word processors and some chat apps turn straight quotation marks into curly ones. Python accepts only straight ones.
So when you copy code from a chat, copy it from the code block, never from formatted text.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you know three errors, and the rule about closing partners. Try the fourth yourself.

after.say: The closing bracket. Every opening bracket needs a closing bracket.
after.heading: Mistake 4: a missing closing bracket

segments.say: Here are all four. Each row starts with the last line of its error report.
Unterminated string literal: a quotation mark is missing.
Name is not defined: check the spelling, such as a capital P.
Invalid character: retype the quotation marks.
Was never closed: add the closing bracket.
So the habit is simple. Read the last line first, then find the line number.

visual.question: An error report has several lines. Which line do you read first?
visual.explain: The last line names the kind of error. Then look for the line number.

segments.say: Quick check. An error report has several lines. Which one do you read first?

after.say: B. The last line. It names the kind of error.

items: Errors are messages, not failures.
Read the last line first.
Then find the line number.
